questions.text: What distinguishes general equilibrium from partial equilibrium analysis?

options.a: General equilibrium always analyzes only one market holding all other prices fixed.
options.b: General equilibrium ignores consumer choices.
options.c: General equilibrium rules out income effects.
options.d: General equilibrium studies mutually connected markets with prices and quantities determined jointly.

questions.text: Why can a supply shock in the coffee market affect the equilibrium price of tea?

options.a: Consumers substitute toward tea when coffee becomes relatively more expensive.
options.b: Coffee and tea must be perfect complements.
options.c: The two prices are technologically identical.
options.d: General equilibrium requires every good to have the same price.

questions.text: If coffee and tea are substitutes and a frost reduces coffee supply, what is a plausible sequence?

options.a: Coffee price falls, tea demand falls, and tea price must be zero.
options.b: Both prices are unchanged because markets are independent.
options.c: Coffee price rises, tea demand increases, tea price rises, feeding back into coffee demand.
options.d: Coffee price stays fixed and tea becomes a complement.

questions.text: Why are endowments central to a pure exchange economy?

options.a: They imply no consumer gains from trade.
options.b: They determine production technology.
options.c: They determine initial goods owned and the market value of consumers' resources.
options.d: They set utility levels directly and prevent trading.

questions.text: What does a pure exchange model exclude?

options.a: Consumers with preferences.
options.b: Trading between consumers.
options.c: The existence of two different goods.
options.d: Production of new goods by firms.

questions.text: Why are competitive price-taking assumptions useful in the exchange model?

options.a: They let consumers choose different market prices for the same good.
options.b: They let each consumer optimize individually at common prices, making market-clearing equilibrium tractable.
options.c: They imply every feasible allocation is automatically efficient.
options.d: They eliminate the budget constraint.

questions.text: What are the dimensions of an Edgeworth box with two goods?

options.a: The marginal rates of substitution.
options.b: Total available quantities of good 1 and good 2.
options.c: The incomes of consumers A and B.
options.d: The two market prices.

questions.text: Where is consumer A's origin in the conventional Edgeworth box?

options.a: The upper-right corner.
options.b: The center of the box.
options.c: The lower-left corner.
options.d: The midpoint of the top edge.

questions.text: Where is consumer B's origin in the conventional Edgeworth box?

options.a: The upper-right corner.
options.b: The center of the box.
options.c: The midpoint of the bottom edge.
options.d: The lower-left corner.

questions.text: What does one point in an Edgeworth box specify?

options.a: The marginal cost of each good.
options.b: A unique set of relative market prices.
options.c: Only consumer A's income, not consumption.
options.d: An allocation of both goods between the two consumers.

questions.text: What does feasibility require for each good in a pure exchange Edgeworth box?

options.a: The market price of each good is zero.
options.b: Total consumption by both people equals total endowment available, for a fully allocated good.
options.c: Each person consumes identical quantities.
options.d: Both consumers have identical utility.

questions.text: In an Edgeworth box, what happens to B's holdings of good 1 when A's holdings rise by one unit at a feasible allocation?

options.a: They fall by one unit.
options.b: They remain unchanged.
options.c: They fall by the price ratio.
options.d: They rise by one unit.

questions.text: Which direction from A's origin usually represents greater consumption of both goods for A?

options.a: Down and to the left.
options.b: Always toward B's origin.
options.c: Along a fixed horizontal line only.
options.d: Up and to the right.

questions.text: Which direction from B's origin usually represents greater consumption of both goods for B?

options.a: Up and to the right from the lower-left corner.
options.b: Toward A's origin only along a diagonal.
options.c: Down and to the left from the upper-right origin.
options.d: Straight up from the upper-right corner.

questions.text: What is the initial endowment point in the Edgeworth box?

options.a: The market equilibrium for every possible price vector.
options.b: The allocation reflecting the goods each consumer owns before trade.
options.c: The allocation that necessarily maximizes both consumers' utilities.
options.d: The intersection of all indifference curves.

questions.text: What is a Pareto improvement?

options.a: Any redistribution that increases aggregate money income.
options.b: An allocation with identical consumption for all people.
options.c: A feasible allocation change that benefits at least one consumer without harming another.
options.d: A change that benefits one consumer even if everyone else loses.

questions.text: What is a Pareto efficient allocation?

options.a: An allocation where no feasible change can make someone better off without making someone else worse off.
options.b: Any allocation with equal incomes.
options.c: An allocation that maximizes every individual's utility separately without resource constraints.
options.d: Any allocation that earns zero profit.

questions.text: What is the lens-shaped region of mutually beneficial trades from an initial interior endowment?

options.a: The region where both consumers have lower utility.
options.b: The entire Edgeworth box.
options.c: The intersection of the areas each consumer strictly prefers to their initial bundle.
options.d: The set of points outside feasibility constraints.

questions.text: Why does a consumer agree to voluntary trade in this model?

options.a: The new bundle is at least as preferred as the endowment, given the opportunity to refuse trade.
options.b: The market requires equal post-trade consumption.
options.c: Prices always force a consumer to buy less of both goods.
options.d: Every trade must lower utility.

questions.text: What is the contract curve or Pareto set?

options.a: The locus of maximum producer profit.
options.b: A line of equal initial endowments.
options.c: The set of all possible market prices.
options.d: The collection of Pareto efficient feasible allocations in the Edgeworth box.

questions.text: At an interior Pareto efficient allocation with smooth preferences, how are the two consumers' marginal rates of substitution related?

options.a: They are equal.
options.b: They must have opposite signs.
options.c: One must be zero.
options.d: They equal the total quantity of goods.

questions.text: Why does equality of marginal rates of substitution matter for Pareto efficiency?

options.a: It requires each person to have the same utility level.
options.b: It forces equal quantities consumed.
options.c: Unequal trade-offs allow mutually beneficial reallocation of goods at an interior point.
options.d: It prevents consumers from exchanging anything at all.

questions.text: Can a Pareto efficient allocation be highly unequal?

options.a: No; efficiency implies equal consumption.
options.b: Yes; Pareto efficiency does not determine whether the allocation is equitable.
options.c: No; all Pareto optima maximize the minimum utility.
options.d: Only if total resources are zero.

questions.text: Why is Pareto efficiency not a criterion for fairness?

options.a: It explicitly demands equal income.
options.b: It judges unexploited mutually beneficial trades rather than the distribution of wellbeing.
options.c: It prohibits unequal initial endowments.
options.d: It ranks all efficient allocations by justice.

questions.text: Can a boundary allocation be Pareto efficient without equal interior marginal rates of substitution?

options.a: No, the equality condition applies universally without exceptions.
options.b: Yes, because interior tangency conditions need not apply at corners.
options.c: No boundary point can be efficient.
options.d: All boundary points are necessarily efficient.

questions.text: What does it mean when all gains from voluntary trade have been exhausted?

options.a: All consumers have consumed their full income without exchanging goods.
options.b: Prices must be zero.
options.c: No mutually beneficial feasible reallocations remain.
options.d: Every agent owns half of each good.

questions.text: What is gross demand for a good by a consumer?

options.a: Only the amount imported from another consumer.
options.b: The total quantity the consumer wishes to consume at given prices and wealth.
options.c: The quantity the consumer initially owns.
options.d: Gross endowment minus total demand.

questions.text: What is net or excess demand for a good by a consumer?

options.a: Market price minus individual income.
options.b: Total resources minus utility.
options.c: Desired consumption minus initial endowment of that good.
options.d: Desired consumption plus initial endowment.

questions.text: If a consumer's net demand for good 1 is negative, what does it mean?

options.a: The consumer's utility is negative.
options.b: The consumer wishes to sell some of good 1.
options.c: The consumer wishes to buy additional good 1.
options.d: The consumer cannot hold good 1.

questions.text: If a consumer's net demand for good 2 is positive, what does it mean?

options.a: The consumer wishes to purchase more of good 2 than initially owned.
options.b: The market price of good 2 is zero.
options.c: The consumer has zero total wealth.
options.d: The consumer must be a net seller of good 2.

questions.text: In a pure exchange economy, how is a consumer's budget wealth determined at market prices?

options.a: Only by the number of goods in the economy.
options.b: By the market value of the consumer's initial endowment.
options.c: By the firm's accounting profit.
options.d: By the sum of all consumers' utility levels.

questions.text: What is market clearing for good 1?

options.a: Aggregate gross demand for good 1 equals its total initial endowment.
options.b: Each consumer has zero gross demand.
options.c: Every consumer demands the same amount of good 1.
options.d: The price of good 1 must equal one.

questions.text: How can equilibrium be expressed using aggregate excess demand functions z1 and z2?

options.a: z1=z2=1 irrespective of endowments.
options.b: z1 times z2 must equal total utility.
options.c: z1 must be positive and z2 negative at equilibrium.
options.d: z1=0 and z2=0 at equilibrium prices.

questions.text: Why can arbitrary prices fail to describe a competitive equilibrium?

options.a: Every positive price vector clears markets.
options.b: Individual optimal choices may generate aggregate excess demand or excess supply.
options.c: Endowments cease to be feasible.
options.d: Consumers are unable to maximize utility at arbitrary positive prices.

questions.text: What is the slope of the common budget line through the endowment point when good 1 is horizontal and good 2 is vertical?

options.b: -MRS_A times MRS_B.

questions.text: At an interior competitive equilibrium with smooth preferences, what relation holds for each consumer?

options.a: Each consumer's MRS equals the common price ratio.
options.b: The consumers' utility levels must be equal.
options.c: The two prices must equal each other.
options.d: Every consumer has identical consumption levels.

questions.text: Why does a common competitive budget line pass through the economy's endowment point?

options.a: Endowments are always on the contract curve.
options.b: The price ratio is fixed by initial utility.
options.c: Consumers necessarily spend zero.
options.d: Total endowment value finances the value of the current allocation at the given prices.

questions.text: What does Walras' law say for a pure exchange economy with budget exhaustion?

options.a: The price-weighted sum of aggregate excess demands equals zero at any positive price vector.
options.b: The total quantity of all goods is infinite.
options.c: Aggregate excess demand for each good is zero at all prices.
options.d: The two goods must have identical prices.

questions.text: Why does Walras' law hold even away from equilibrium?

options.a: Every person buys exactly what they originally owned.
options.b: Every market clears automatically.
options.c: Consumers' budget identities imply the value of what they demand equals the value of their endowments, in aggregate.
options.d: A central planner forces demand to equal supply.

questions.text: In a two-good pure exchange economy with positive prices, if market 1 clears and Walras' law holds, what follows?

options.a: Market 2 also clears.
options.b: Market 2 must have strictly positive excess demand.
options.c: The consumers must have equal utilities.
options.d: Market 2 must have negative price.

questions.text: If p1 z1 + p2 z2=0 with positive prices and z1 is strictly positive, what must hold for z2?

options.a: It is strictly positive.
options.b: It is strictly negative.
options.c: It is zero.
options.d: It is necessarily equal to z1.

questions.text: Why is only one independent market-clearing equation needed to find a relative equilibrium price in a two-good exchange economy?

options.a: One good has no demand.
options.b: The two markets never interact.
options.c: Walras' law makes the second condition redundant when the first holds.
options.d: Both goods always have the same price.

questions.text: Why can one good's price be normalized to one when solving a competitive pure exchange equilibrium?

options.a: Only relative prices matter for consumers' homogeneous budget-constrained demands.
options.b: The good has zero production cost.
options.c: One good is necessarily free.
options.d: Absolute prices uniquely determine real endowments.

questions.text: Does Walras' law assert that every market clears at every positive price vector?

options.a: Yes, market clearing is automatic for all goods.
options.b: Yes, if the budget is exhausted, every single net demand is zero.
options.c: Only when both goods are perfect complements.
options.d: No; it only states that the aggregate value of excess demands sums to zero.

questions.text: What is the first fundamental theorem of welfare economics?

options.a: A competitive equilibrium allocation is Pareto efficient under the standard assumptions.
options.b: Every Pareto efficient allocation must emerge without redistribution from any endowment.
options.c: All competitive equilibria have equal welfare.
options.d: Monopolies necessarily yield Pareto efficiency.

questions.text: Why does the first welfare theorem rely on individual utility maximization at competitive prices?

options.a: It requires zero total goods available.
options.b: A Pareto-improving feasible allocation would contradict affordability and optimality for consumers at equilibrium.
options.c: It assumes consumers maximize producer profits.
options.d: It requires all consumers to have identical preferences.

questions.text: What does the first welfare theorem not establish?

options.a: That the resulting allocation is fair or yields an equal distribution.
options.b: That all feasible Pareto improvements have been exhausted.
options.c: That market equilibrium can be Pareto efficient under assumptions.
options.d: That the competitive equilibrium can lie on the contract curve.

questions.text: Which market failure can undermine the simple first welfare theorem's conclusion?

options.a: Smooth preferences and common competitive prices.
options.b: Complete markets with price taking.
options.c: Budget exhaustion with feasible allocation.
options.d: An externality or market power that prevents prices from capturing the relevant trade-offs.

questions.text: What is the second fundamental theorem of welfare economics?

options.a: Every initial endowment produces the same equilibrium allocation.
options.b: Redistribution is never relevant to welfare economics.
options.c: Competitive equilibrium always yields equal incomes.
options.d: Under suitable convexity and related assumptions, a Pareto efficient allocation can be supported as a competitive equilibrium after appropriate redistribution of endowments.

questions.text: What is the role of lump-sum redistribution in the second welfare theorem?

options.a: It guarantees a unique social preference ranking.
options.b: It sets different prices for each consumer.
options.c: It changes the technological marginal products.
options.d: It changes initial purchasing power without distorting marginal market trade-offs.

questions.text: Why are convex preferences important for the second welfare theorem's decentralization result?

options.a: They ensure every consumer has identical endowments.
options.b: They imply that every firm is a monopolist.
options.c: They help support Pareto efficient allocations by a common price line.
options.d: They eliminate all corner solutions automatically.

questions.text: What is the distinction between the two welfare theorems?

options.a: Both claim that prices have no allocative role.
options.b: The first runs from competitive equilibrium to efficiency; the second runs from suitable efficient allocations to supporting prices and redistribution.
options.c: Both state that any unequal allocation is inefficient.
options.d: The first requires monopoly; the second requires monopsony.

questions.text: How can policy conceptually separate efficiency and distribution under the second welfare theorem's assumptions?

options.a: Ban all voluntary trade.
options.b: Maximize each consumer's utility independently of feasibility.
options.c: Mandate unequal marginal prices for identical goods.
options.d: Redistribute endowments with lump-sum transfers, then let competitive markets allocate resources.

questions.text: Can a Pareto efficient allocation fail to be a competitive equilibrium from the original endowments?

options.a: No; every efficient allocation is an equilibrium from every endowment.
options.b: Yes; it may require a different initial wealth distribution to be supported by competitive trade.
options.c: Only if prices are zero for every good.
options.d: No; the contract curve contains exactly one point.

questions.text: If both consumers maximize utility and trade at the same prices at an interior equilibrium, what helps prove its Pareto efficiency?

options.a: Each has identical gross demand.
options.b: The total endowment must increase through trade.
options.c: Their MRS values both equal the common price ratio, so no beneficial marginal exchange remains.
options.d: Their utility levels must be equal.

questions.text: Why is a Pareto improvement infeasible at a competitive equilibrium under the standard first-theorem conditions?

options.a: To improve at least one consumer without harming others would require more aggregate value of goods than the economy possesses.
options.b: All prices are necessarily zero.
options.c: Each consumer must own the same bundle.
options.d: An equilibrium uses no scarce resources.

questions.text: What can a contract curve contain in an exchange economy?

options.a: Only the unique point with equal incomes.
options.b: All points in the box regardless of efficiency.
options.c: Only allocations where nobody consumes good 1.
options.d: Multiple efficient allocations reflecting different distributions of available goods.

questions.text: In the Edgeworth box pictured, which pair correctly identifies the consumers' origins?

options.a: Both at the midpoint of the box.
options.b: A at upper right and B at lower left.
options.c: A at lower left and B at upper right.
options.d: Both at lower left.
